title: JavaScript 事件循环详解：队列跟踪与调试指南
author: SitePoint Team
content:
A developer schedules a Promise.resolve().then(...) and a setTimeout(..., 0) in the same synchronous block. The promise callback fires first. They expected the timer. The bug that follows can take extended debugging because the order only matters under specific interleaving conditions. This scenario is common, and having the JavaScript event loop explained at a conceptual level does not prevent it.

By the end of this article, readers will manually trace any async snippet through the call stack, microtask queue, and task queue, and predict the exact output order. The article delivers: annotated code snippets with expected output, queue trace tables that map every scheduling decision step by step, and a browser vs. Node.js comparison table grounded in the current HTML Living Standard event loop processing model.

Table of Contents

  • Why "Knowing" the Event Loop Isn't Enough
  • The Browser Event Loop Model: What the Spec Actually Says
  • Queue Tracing: A Step-by-Step Method
  • Trace Example 1: Promises vs. setTimeout
  • Trace Example 2: Nested Microtasks and Microtask Starvation
  • Browser vs. Node.js Event Loop: Key Differences
  • Debugging Async Code in Practice
  • Key Takeaways and Quick-Reference Rules

Why "Knowing" the Event Loop Isn't Enough

A developer schedules a Promise.resolve().then(...) and a setTimeout(..., 0) in the same synchronous block. The promise callback fires first. They expected the timer. The bug that follows can take extended debugging because the order only matters under specific interleaving conditions. This scenario is common, and having the JavaScript event loop explained at a conceptual level does not prevent it.

By the end of this article, readers will manually trace any async snippet through the call stack, microtask queue, and task queue, and predict the exact output order. The target audience is intermediate JavaScript developers who write promises and async/await comfortably but remain fuzzy on the underlying execution mechanics that determine when callbacks actually run.

The article delivers: annotated code snippets with expected output, queue trace tables that map every scheduling decision step by step, and a browser vs. Node.js comparison table grounded in the current HTML Living Standard event loop processing model.

The Browser Event Loop Model: What the Spec Actually Says

Task Sources and the Task Queue

The HTML Living Standard defines a "task" (often called a macrotask in informal usage) as a unit of work dispatched from a specific task source. Key task sources enumerated in the spec include DOM manipulation, user interaction events, networking (such as XMLHttpRequest and fetch response handling), history traversal, and timer callbacks from setTimeout and setInterval.

A detail that most simplified diagrams omit: the specification allows multiple task queues. Each task source can have its own queue, and the browser's event loop implementation chooses one task from one queue per iteration. The spec leaves the selection algorithm to the implementation, which means browsers can prioritize user interaction tasks over timer tasks within the same loop iteration. The spec requires only that tasks from the same source execute in order relative to each other, not that all task queues share a single FIFO ordering.

This means a setTimeout callback and a click event handler are not guaranteed to interleave in any particular order beyond their respective source orderings. Understanding this removes a class of false assumptions about deterministic timer behavior.

The Microtask Checkpoint

After each task completes, and when the call stack empties at the end of script evaluation, the event loop performs a microtask checkpoint that fully drains the microtask queue before moving on. The term "fully drains" is precise and consequential: if a microtask enqueues another microtask during the checkpoint, that new microtask is also processed within the same checkpoint cycle.

The microtask checkpoint also runs when the call stack empties at the end of the initial script evaluation, not only after a prior task has completed. This is why, in the trace examples below, microtasks fire after synchronous code finishes even though no preceding task triggered them.

Three primary mechanisms enqueue microtasks: Promise.then/catch/finally callbacks on settled promises, explicit calls to queueMicrotask() (supported in Chrome 71+, Firefox 69+, Safari 12.1+; not available in IE11), and MutationObserver notification callbacks. Other mechanisms, such as async/await continuations (which desugar to promise callbacks), also enqueue microtasks. The draining behavior means that a chain of microtasks that continually enqueues more work will prevent the event loop from ever reaching the next task or a rendering step.

The microtask checkpoint algorithm is specified directly in the HTML Standard. It runs not only after tasks but also after certain callback steps and when the call stack is empty during script execution cleanup.

Rendering and requestAnimationFrame

Rendering fits into the loop iteration after the microtask checkpoint. The browser updates rendering roughly every 16 ms on 60 Hz displays (on 90/120/144 Hz displays the frame budget is proportionally shorter: approximately 11 ms, 8 ms, or 7 ms), though it can skip iterations. requestAnimationFrame callbacks execute before the paint step, but only on iterations where the browser elects to render; if the browser skips a render step, rAF callbacks are also skipped on that iteration. This placement ensures that animation logic runs as close to the actual frame as possible, avoiding the timing drift (often 4-16 ms per frame) that setTimeout-based animation loops suffer from.

Queue Tracing: A Step-by-Step Method

The trace table method uses four columns: Step, Call Stack, Microtask Queue, and Task Queue. At every meaningful point in execution, the reader records what enters and exits each column: function calls pushed onto the stack, callbacks scheduled into microtask or task queues, and the moment each callback is dequeued and executed.

Walk through the code line by line. When a synchronous call occurs, push it onto the Call Stack column. When Promise.resolve().then(cb) appears, place cb in the Microtask Queue column; similarly, setTimeout(cb, 0) goes into the Task Queue column. When the call stack empties, drain all entries in the Microtask Queue column before pulling the next entry from the Task Queue column.

This manual technique mirrors what browser-based event loop visualizers do programmatically, but building the tables by hand develops the intuition needed to predict behavior without tooling.

Trace Example 1: Promises vs. setTimeout

The Code

console.log('1: script start');

setTimeout(function () {
  console.log('2: setTimeout');
}, 0);

Promise.resolve()
  .then(function () {
    console.log('3: promise 1');
  })
  .then(function () {
    console.log('4: promise 2');
  });

console.log('5: script end');

This event loop in JavaScript example demonstrates that microtasks (promise callbacks) execute before macrotasks (setTimeout) even when both are scheduled during the same synchronous block.

Step-by-Step Queue Trace Table

At Step 4, the synchronous script finishes. The call stack empties. At Step 5, the microtask checkpoint begins and drains cb1. Because cb1's .then(cb2) chain was registered during initial scheduling, cb2 enters the microtask queue when cb1's promise resolves. Step 6 drains cb2 within the same checkpoint. Only at Step 7 does the event loop pull from the task queue.

Expected Output (Annotated)

1: script start    // Synchronous — runs immediately on the call stack
5: script end      // Synchronous — runs before any async callback
3: promise 1       // Microtask — drained before any task queue entry
4: promise 2       // Microtask — enqueued by prior .then(), drained in same checkpoint
2: setTimeout      // Task — runs only after microtask queue is empty

Trace Example 2: Nested Microtasks and Microtask Starvation

The Code

console.log('start');

setTimeout(function () {
  console.log('timeout');
}, 0);

function chainMicrotasks(count) {
  // Guard: treat non-finite or non-integer input as 0
  if (!Number.isFinite(count) || count <= 0) return;
  Promise.resolve().then(function () {
    console.log('microtask ' + count);
    // Recursive call is async — re-enters via microtask queue, not call stack
    chainMicrotasks(count - 1);
  });
}

chainMicrotasks(5);

console.log('end');

This snippet demonstrates microtask starvation in a controlled fashion. Each .then() callback enqueues another .then(), keeping the microtask queue populated across five iterations. The setTimeout callback waits in the task queue until all microtasks complete. With a larger count (or no decrement at all), the timeout callback would be delayed indefinitely, and in a browser context, rendering would be blocked entirely.

Step-by-Step Queue Trace Table

The task queue entry cb waits from Step 2 through Step 9. If chainMicrotasks never decremented, the microtask queue would refill on every drain step, and 'timeout' would never print.

How to Detect and Fix Starvation

Symptoms in a browser include UI freezes, unresponsive click handlers, and setTimeout callbacks delayed indefinitely. In the Chrome DevTools Performance panel, microtask starvation appears as a single extremely long "Task" bar with no rendering frames interleaved.

The fix is to break long microtask chains by yielding to the task queue. Replace the recursive Promise.resolve().then(...) pattern with setTimeout(..., 0) at periodic intervals, which forces the next iteration into the task queue and allows rendering and other tasks to proceed. Where available, await scheduler.yield() is the purpose-built way to yield to the task queue and continue afterward (it is supported in Chromium browsers and Firefox 142+, but not Safari, per Can I use). Otherwise, setTimeout works but browsers throttle it in background tabs, and MessageChannel is a common alternative for foreground yielding. For non-urgent background work in browsers, requestIdleCallback offers a way to schedule work only when the browser is idle. The long task threshold in Chrome DevTools is 50 ms; tasks exceeding this duration are flagged and are strong candidates for starvation investigation.

Browser vs. Node.js Event Loop: Key Differences

Node.js Event Loop Phases

The Node.js event loop, explained in terms of its underlying architecture, runs on libuv (the cross-platform async I/O library underlying Node.js) and operates in six distinct phases: timers, pending callbacks, idle/prepare, poll, check, and close callbacks. This is structurally different from the browser's single-iteration model defined in the HTML Standard.

process.nextTick callbacks occupy a separate queue that drains before promise microtasks. Resolved promise callbacks and queueMicrotask callbacks drain after process.nextTick but before moving to the next phase. This behavior applies to all current Node.js LTS releases (v18+); it was introduced in v11.0.0. Since that change, microtasks drain between every callback within a phase, not just between phases, which aligned Node.js behavior more closely with browser semantics.

setImmediate executes in the check phase, which occurs after the poll phase. setTimeout(..., 0) executes in the timers phase. When both are scheduled from within the poll phase (such as inside an I/O callback), setImmediate consistently fires first. When scheduled from the main module (outside I/O), the ordering between setImmediate and setTimeout(..., 0) is non-deterministic and depends on system timer resolution.

Comparison Table

Code Example: Divergent Output

// Node.js only — run with: node snippet.js
// Throws ReferenceError in browsers: process and setImmediate are not defined.
if (typeof process === 'undefined' || typeof setImmediate === 'undefined') {
  throw new Error('This snippet requires Node.js. Do not run in a browser.');
}

setTimeout(() => console.log('setTimeout'), 0);
setImmediate(() => console.log('setImmediate'));       // Node.js only — check phase
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('promise'));
process.nextTick(() => console.log('nextTick'));       // Node.js only — nextTick queue
console.log('sync');

/*
  Expected output when run as a CommonJS script on Node.js 18+ (lines 1-3 are deterministic; lines 4-5 are not).
  As an ES module, 'promise' prints before 'nextTick':
    sync
    nextTick
    promise
    [setTimeout or setImmediate — order varies between runs when called from main module]
    [setImmediate or setTimeout — the other one]
*/

Browser output (subset that runs):

sync          // Synchronous
promise       // Microtask checkpoint
setTimeout    // Task queue

In a CommonJS script, process.nextTick callbacks run before promise microtasks. In an ES module (for example a .mjs file), the order flips for code that runs at the top level of the module: promise prints before nextTick, because the module itself is evaluated inside a promise job. The sample above was run on Node 22 in both forms. In the browser, no equivalent queue exists, so promise callbacks are the highest-priority async mechanism after the synchronous call stack clears.

Debugging Async Code in Practice

When a breakpoint lands inside a .then() and you need the originating call chain

Open the Sources panel in Chrome DevTools. When you pause at a breakpoint inside a .then() callback, the Call Stack pane can show the async frames that led there, not just the frame that is running now. This is the fastest path to understanding why a particular async callback fired.

Chrome DevTools: Performance Panel for Long Tasks

Record a performance trace, filter for tasks longer than 50 ms (the Long Task threshold), and look for microtask-heavy frames. Microtask starvation shows up as a single extremely long "Task" bar with no rendering frames interleaved. The Performance panel is the primary tool for identifying whether expensive synchronous work or runaway microtask chains are blocking the event loop.

Node.js: --inspect, Async Hooks, and Diagnostic Reports

Attaching the Node.js inspector with --inspect-brk enables Chrome DevTools for server-side code, including full async stack traces. This is the most accessible way to debug async ordering issues in Node.js without modifying application code.

The async_hooks module traces async resource lifecycles programmatically, tracking when async operations are initialized, called, and destroyed. The overhead is measurable: profile before enabling in production, and consult the Node.js async_hooks documentation for current performance guidance. Consider AsyncLocalStorage or diagnostics_channel as lower-overhead alternatives for production observability.

For capturing event loop utilization snapshots, process.report.writeReport(), or the --report-on-signal and --report-uncaught-exception flags, generate JSON diagnostic reports with JavaScript and native stacks, active libuv handles, and resource usage.

Common Async Bugs and Their Queue-Level Explanations

This pattern is broken; do not copy it:

// Browser only: the relative URL '/api/data' is not valid in Node.js
let result = null;

fetch('/api/data')
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(data => {
    result = data;
  });

console.log(result); // null — always

The synchronous console.log(result) executes while still on the call stack. The .then() callbacks are in the microtask queue, waiting for the stack to clear. Even if the fetch resolved instantly, result would still be null at that line: network response delivery arrives as a task from the network task source, and only the .then() callbacks are microtasks, neither of which has run yet.

Corrected version:

// Browser only: the relative URL '/api/data' is not valid in Node.js
let result = null;

fetch('/api/data')
  .then(function (response) {
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error('HTTP error: ' + response.status);
    }
    return response.json();
  })
  .then(function (data) {
    result = data;
    console.log(result); // Correct place to read result — inside the chain
  })
  .catch(function (err) {
    console.error('Fetch failed:', err.message);
  });

// This still logs null — synchronous code runs before any microtask
console.log(result);

The corrected version guards against non-2xx HTTP responses (since fetch only rejects on network failure, not on HTTP error status) and includes a .catch() handler to prevent unhandled promise rejections, which crash the process in Node.js 15+ and fire silent unhandledrejection events in browsers.

Common pitfalls that the queue model explains directly:

  • The synchronous code path finishes before any microtask runs, so reading a value set inside a promise chain from synchronous code always returns the initial value.
  • The microtask queue drains entirely before the task queue is consulted, which is why setTimeout(..., 0) never fires before a promise callback scheduled in the same turn.
  • Each microtask that enqueues another microtask extends the checkpoint indefinitely. Recursive promise chains without yielding to the task queue will starve rendering and I/O.
  • Outside I/O callbacks in Node.js, the ordering between setImmediate and setTimeout(..., 0) is non-deterministic due to system timer resolution. Don't rely on a specific order unless you're inside an I/O callback.

Key Takeaways and Quick-Reference Rules

  1. After each task completes, and after the initial script evaluation ends, the event loop drains all microtasks before dequeuing the next task.
  2. Microtasks enqueued during the microtask checkpoint drain within the same checkpoint, not deferred to a later one.
  3. Don't assume rAF runs every frame. Rendering happens after the microtask checkpoint only on iterations where the browser elects to render, and requestAnimationFrame callbacks run before paint on those iterations. On 60 Hz displays this is roughly every 16 ms; higher refresh rates shorten the budget proportionally.
  4. In Node.js (v11+, including all current LTS releases), microtasks drain between each callback within a phase, not just between phases.
  5. Watch out for process.nextTick in Node.js: its callbacks drain before promise microtasks in CommonJS code, forming a separate higher-priority queue that can itself cause starvation.
  6. If the microtask queue never empties, the UI (browser) or I/O processing (Node.js) starves.

The canonical references for further depth are the HTML Living Standard event loop processing model and the Node.js event loop documentation.

summary: 本文深入探讨了 JavaScript 事件循环的机制，解释了异步任务是如何被调度和执行的。文章详细介绍了浏览器的事件循环模型，包括任务源和微任务检查点的区别。指南中包含了一些实用的队列跟踪示例，用于预测执行顺序，并讨论了浏览器与 Node.js 事件循环之间的差异。此外，文章还提供了用于调试异步代码的策略，例如识别 promise 回调的来源以及检测微任务饥饿现象。

mainPoints.point: 浏览器事件循环在单一的迭代周期内运行，从各种源（例如，计时器和 DOM 事件）处理任务，并在每个任务完成后清空微任务队列。
mainPoints.explanation: HTML 活标准规定了事件循环为不断重复的循环，其中浏览器会检查任务、执行它们，然后在继续下一个任务之前处理任何待决的微任务（例如，promise 回调）。这确保了微任务的优先级高于常规任务。

mainPoints.point: 队列跟踪是一种手动的方法，用于通过在每个步骤跟踪调用栈、微任务队列和任务队列的状态来预测异步代码的执行顺序。
mainPoints.explanation: 通过有条理地记录推入到调用栈中的内容以及安排到队列中的内容，开发者可以可视化执行流。这有助于识别可能存在的问题，例如竞态条件或意外的回调顺序。

mainPoints.point: Node.js 事件循环与浏览器有所不同，具有不同的阶段，并为 process.nextTick 回调保留了单独的队列。
mainPoints.explanation: Node.js 使用基于阶段的模型，其中事件循环会经过特定的阶段，例如，timers、I/O 和 check。process.nextTick 队列中的内容在 promise 微任务之前被执行，这意味着与浏览器环境相比，执行顺序可能会有所不同。

mainPoints.point: 微任务饥饿发生在微任务链条阻断事件循环进入任务队列或渲染步骤时，导致 UI 冻结。
mainPoints.explanation: 如果一个 promise 回调反复向微任务队列中添加新的微任务而没有让步，则微任务队列永远不会变空。这将阻塞其他任务（例如，setTimeout 回调）的执行，并阻止浏览器渲染更新，导致界面冻结。

keyQuotes: 这个 bug 很难排查，因为顺序只有在特定的交错条件下才重要。
微任务检查点会在调用栈在初始脚本评估的末尾变空时运行，而不仅仅是在先前的任务完成后。
解决方法是把长微任务链拆开，让它们让步给任务队列。
Node.js 事件循环基于底层架构，运行在 libuv 上，并分为六个不同的阶段。
在 Chrome 开发工具的性能面板中，微任务饥饿表现为一个非常长的 'Task' 条，其中没有交错的渲染帧。
